projects.title: Work
projects.description: dev-skills: an agent workflow from requirement to mergeable PR.
projects.leadHtml:
A set of Skills that takes a requirement to a mergeable PR.
These are my public projects.
projects.touchpoints: You step in at three points: confirm the decisions, confirm the acceptance criteria, and read the decision list before you merge.
projects.flowCaption: {count} Skills in all; four of them carry a requirement through to merge

devSkills.flowIntro: Each repository is prepared once. After that, every requirement goes through definition and delivery. Gaps a run exposes in the repository are listed in the PR, and you decide whether to address them in the repository or in the Skills.
devSkills.flowNote: A few rules hold throughout. Every decision a person has to make, and every acceptance requirement, is settled at the start. At the end, a model from another family verifies against the acceptance criteria. In between, one owner does the work. Irreversible operations stay with you: merging, force-pushing a shared branch, deleting shared data, sending external messages, changing a shared environment.
devSkills.supportIntro: Reviews, PR reading and reports in the workflow use these three Skills. Each also works on its own.
devSkills.standaloneIntro: Not part of the delivery workflow. Call them for the task at hand.
installParagraphsHtml: Installed as a plugin, the Skills are namespaced: /dev-skills:core-grill in MCode and Claude Code, $dev-skills:core-grill in Codex. Linked from a clone, they have no namespace: /core-grill or $core-grill. Use one or the other, not both.

In Claude Code and Codex, the agent can also call core-spec on its own once a discussion is finished; the other Skills are manual-only. MCode doesn't read that setting yet, so calling Skills by name is the safer choice.
prereqParagraphsHtml: You need CLIs for models from two different families, installed and logged in; by default, Claude Code and Codex. The gap check and the final verification must come from the other family. With only one family available, the workflow stops at that step instead of checking with the same family.

You also need Node.js 24, git, and gh or glab for PRs, plus an app the agent can start, operate and observe from a worktree, which is what repo-readiness sets up. Plugin installs cover MCode, Claude Code and Codex; end-to-end tests have only been run in Claude Code and Codex.

about.title: About
about.description: I'm Shijie Xie. I build coding agents at MiniMax and write about using them for real work.
about.h1Html:
I build coding agents,
and ship my own work with them.
about.lead: I'm Shijie Xie. I build coding agents at MiniMax, then use them to ship my own work. Been through every shift in AI coding: prompts, context, harness. This site keeps my public work and the notes from each.
about.careTitle: What I keep coming back to
careParagraphs: Across several jobs, I've kept coming back to one question: how can developers get more done? From developer productivity to code intelligence to AI coding, the tools changed, and so did the calls I had to make.
These days I care most about how an agent gets the right context, how its results get verified, and how mistakes surface while it's still running.

projects.summary: From requirement to a verified, mergeable PR: a set of Skills for coding agents.
projects.detail: First, give the repository a verification environment the agent can start, operate and observe on its own. After that, one agent takes each requirement from start to finish and proves the result in the running app, and a model from another family verifies it independently. You step in at three points: confirm the decisions, confirm the acceptance criteria, and read the decision list before you merge.
projects.updateNote: dev-skills · rewritten around the requirement-to-PR workflow

catalog.name: repo-readiness
catalog.title: Let agents verify on their own
catalog.description: Done once per repository. Sets up the project's own verification Skill: agents can start, operate and observe the app from its own worktree, with feature maps of numbered criteria, scenario scripts, smoke tests, and a structure check in CI. Whatever the repository can't answer, it asks you in one batch.
catalog.you: once per repository, answer what the repository can't tell it
catalog.example: /dev-skills:repo-readiness The next requirement is <link or text>

catalog.name: core-grill
catalog.title: Ask what only you can decide
catalog.description: At the start of a requirement, asks in rounds about the decisions that change what users see: interactions, copy, defaults, entry points, whether data can be lost. Each question comes with options, consequences and a recommendation. The agent settles implementation details itself and records them as defaults. It ends with a decision summary.
catalog.you: answer the questions and confirm the decision summary once
catalog.example: /dev-skills:core-grill The requirement is <link or text>; put the requirement documents in <requirement directory>/

catalog.name: core-spec
catalog.title: Write down decisions and acceptance criteria
catalog.description: Turns the decision summary into spec.md (decisions and constraints) and verify.md (acceptance requirements), and has a model from another family check them clause by clause. Once you confirm, both files are frozen and committed to the feature branch, and a draft PR is opened. It can also produce just spec.md.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:core-spec Write spec.md and verify.md from the decision summary

catalog.name: deliver
catalog.title: One agent, all the way to a mergeable PR
catalog.description: From the frozen spec and verify, one owner implements milestone by milestone and runs the scenarios in the running app. Before a decision, it consults a model from another family, then makes the call and lists it at the top of the PR. Finally, a model from another family verifies the final code independently, and the owner works through CI and review until the PR can be merged.
catalog.you: read the decision list before merging, then merge

catalog.name: review-rules
catalog.title: Review against clear criteria
catalog.description: Five criteria for reviewing code and designs, re-checking review comments and judging fixes: correct and complete, the minimal necessary change, complexity that matches the benefit, enough extensibility, and a clear division of responsibilities.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:review-rules Re-check this review comment: what's the basis, and what's the smallest fix?

catalog.name: mr-for-human
catalog.title: Read the code an agent wrote
catalog.description: Turns a PR into a reading guide for people: first the core conclusions and what needs your judgment, then the design, the execution logic in pseudocode and the runtime constraints, and finally where to find the code.

catalog.name: explain-as-fool
catalog.title: Explain it plainly
catalog.description: Explains a topic to someone who knows nothing about it, directly and without rhetoric. Reports that other Skills write for people follow its writing rules.

catalog.name: design-for-review
catalog.title: A design people can review
catalog.description: Turns requirements and design material into a self-contained technical review document: the problem, the overall design, the scope of the change and the trade-offs that need a decision.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:design-for-review Turn the confirmed design into a review document

catalog.name: plan-for-agents
catalog.title: Turn decisions into a plan
catalog.description: Creates, revises or checks a complete plan for agents to execute, from requirements and confirmed decisions down to steps, outputs and acceptance evidence.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:plan-for-agents Write a self-contained plan from the confirmed spec

catalog.name: agent-prompt-rules
catalog.title: Rules for writing to agents
catalog.description: Rules for writing and reviewing prompts for agents, multi-agent pipelines and SKILL.md files, each linked to the Anthropic or OpenAI source it rests on.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:agent-prompt-rules Review this SKILL.md against the rules

catalog.name: recon-to-contract
catalog.title: Turn research into a contract
catalog.description: Turns a comparison of two or more external references into one executable contract with evidence, decisions and acceptance criteria.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:recon-to-contract Compare these three open-source implementations and produce a migration contract

articles.title: I stopped babysitting my coding agents. Here's the workflow.
articles.summary: One eight-module job took 14 hours, and for about 76% of it only one CLI was working. What I learned from OpenAI, Anthropic and Lauren Tan, and the workflow and three skills I use now.

contributions.title: A slowdown, or a noisy machine?
contributions.summary: Paired re-runs in performance CI, to tell a real regression apart from runner noise and from too little evidence.
contributions.detail: The performance budgets stay the same. Routine checks warn on persistent noise; the full performance check still needs a clear result.
